name: Tang Seng Rou (唐僧肉)
blurb: "Tang Monk meat": a meatless spicy flour snack sold for a few jiao outside schools
title: What Is Tang Seng Rou (唐僧肉)? The Chinese Childhood Snack
description: Tang Seng Rou ("Tang Monk meat") was a cheap Chinese school-gate snack of the 1990s and 2000s: no meat, just seasoned flour strips or fried chips.
h1: What is Tang Seng Rou (唐僧肉)?
answer: Tang Seng Rou, literally "Tang Monk meat", was a cheap snack sold at shops outside Chinese schools from roughly the 1990s into the 2000s. Despite the name it contained no meat: it was usually a spicy-sweet seasoned flour or soy product, or a fried or puffed chip, sold for a few jiao (a fraction of a yuan) a bag. It was a name many small makers used rather than one brand. After crackdowns on unlicensed "five-mao snacks", the old workshop versions mostly vanished, though licensed companies still sell spicy strips under the name.

body: The name is a joke from Journey to the West, the classic novel that every Chinese child knew from the TV series: in the story, demons want to eat the monk Tang Seng because his flesh supposedly grants immortality. A snack called "Tang Monk meat" was instantly memorable to kids. No one knows exactly who used the name first.

What was inside the bag varied by region and maker. Many people remember chewy, sweet-and-spicy strips of seasoned wheat gluten, the same family as latiao; others remember crunchy fried chips. A 2015 China News Service report grouped Tang Seng Rou with snacks like "mushroom beef" that had "a meat name but no meat": fried, puffed or seasoned flour products in small, often greasy plastic bags, sometimes printed with Journey to the West characters.

head: When
What happened
rows: Common at small shops and stalls near schools, sold for a few jiao a bag
After several major food-safety cases, regulators cracked down on unlabelled workshop snacks
Chinese media report widely on "five-mao snacks"; Tang Seng Rou is named as a meat-named, meatless type
Beijing runs a campaign against five-mao snacks, citing odd names like Tang Seng Rou; wholesale markets pull them
Regulators classify latiao-type products as convenience food (seasoned flour products) under licensing

body: "Five-mao snacks" (wumao lingshi) is the media's umbrella term for these: latiao, spicy slices, dried fruit and puffed snacks typically sold for 0.5 to 1 yuan a bag.
The name survives. Licensed manufacturers still make sweet-and-spicy gluten strips labelled Tang Seng Rou, produced and labelled as seasoned flour products.
They are not the same snack people remember, because there never was one recipe: every small factory made its own. The unlabelled workshop bags of the 1990s are essentially gone from regular retail.

ul: Joking that eating it would make you immortal, like the demons in the story
Paying in jiao, with change from lunch money
Shelf-mates with equally misleading names, such as "mushroom beef"
Bags that soaked through with chili oil and left red fingertips

faq.q: Does Tang Seng Rou contain meat?
faq.a: No. It was made mainly from flour or soy with oil, chili and seasonings; the name is a joke from Journey to the West.

faq.q: Is Tang Seng Rou the same as latiao?
faq.a: Many versions were latiao-type seasoned flour strips, but some were fried chips. Since many makers used the name, it varied.
Tang Monk meat. In Journey to the West, demons hunt the monk Tang Seng because eating him was said to grant immortality.
